text.text: <atomic>Lindsey grew roses for a flower shop. One day, she noticed tumor-like growths on her rose stems.</atomic>

<atomic>She read a book about plant diseases and learned that the plants had crown gall disease, which is caused by a type of bacteria. She also read that allicin, a chemical found in garlic, can kill bacteria.</atomic>
<atomic>She was curious if garlic could prevent more tumors from forming on her plants.</atomic>
<atomic>Lindsey sprayed garlic juice on ten infected plants and water on another ten.</atomic>
<atomic>After one month, she compared the number of new tumors on plants in each group and found no difference between them.</atomic>
<atomic>Lindsey thought that the concentration of allicin in her garlic spray might be too low, so spraying the plants with pure allicin would decrease the number of new tumors.</atomic>
<atomic>She repeated her experiment, this time spraying the plants with a solution of pure allicin.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Julia pushed Emily and Emily's little brother, Mateo, on swings.</atomic>
<atomic>Julia noticed that Mateo always swung back in less time than Emily.</atomic>
<atomic>Julia asked Emily if she thought the weight on a swing was related to the time it took to return.</atomic>
<atomic>To find out, Emily stood back four feet and released a swing three times, once with a light weight attached to it, once with a medium weight, and once with a heavy weight.</atomic>
<atomic>Julia measured how long it took the swing to go forward and back each time.</atomic>
<atomic>They repeated the tests on ten swings.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided that weight on a swing wasn't related to swinging time, since for each swing the time was similar with all three weights.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, Julia noticed that swings with shorter chains always swung back sooner.</atomic>
<atomic>She thought that chain length would determine swinging time and that shortening a swing's chains would shorten the time it took to swing back.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Every morning, Harry watched hummingbirds in his garden. He wanted to get a feeder to attract more hummingbirds.</atomic>
<atomic>He noticed that hummingbirds often drank nectar from brightly colored flowers.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the color of the feeder would influence how often hummingbirds visited it.</atomic>
<atomic>Harry hung a red feeder next to a white feeder in three locations around his garden. Every day for a week, he spent an hour tallying the number of hummingbird visits to each feeder.</atomic>
<atomic>At the end of the week, he compared the average number of visits to each feeder, and he found that there were more visits to the red feeders than to the white feeders.</atomic>
<atomic>Harry deduced that the red feeders were more attractive to hummingbirds than the white feeders.</atomic>
<atomic>He decided to repeat his experiment to determine if feeders painted other bright colors, such as orange and yellow, would also attract hummingbirds.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Cole was a line cook in a restaurant, and he was making a new pasta dish.</atomic>
<atomic>The recipe instructed him to add salt to the pasta-cooking water.</atomic>
<atomic>Cole knew that adding salt to water would cause the water to reach a higher temperature before it boiled.</atomic>
<atomic>Because pasta should cook faster at a higher temperature, Cole speculated that the added salt would make the pasta cook more quickly.</atomic>
<atomic>Cole made four pots of pasta with salted water and another four pots with unsalted water.</atomic>
<atomic>He compared the amount of time it took the pasta to cook to see if it cooked faster in pots with salt.</atomic>
<atomic>His results showed that although the water from the salted pots boiled at a slightly hotter temperature, the pasta cooked at similar rates in all the pots.</atomic>
<atomic>He discussed the results of the experiment with his coworkers.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided not to bother adding salt to the pasta water.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Jim likes to make rock candy to share with his friends.</atomic>
<atomic>He normally makes rock candy using white sugar but wondered if he could make larger sugar crystals using pure cane sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that pure cane sugar would make the largest crystals, since it was a more pure form of sugar.</atomic>

<atomic>Jim set up 12 glass jars with a stick and hot water. He added white sugar to 6 jars and pure cane sugar to the other 6. After one week, Jim measured the size of the sugar crystals in each jar.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the rock candy made with white sugar had larger crystals than those made with pure cane sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He then predicted that smaller sugar granules would lead to larger sugar crystals.</atomic>

<atomic>This made him consider whether his basil plants were not growing many leaves because their soil lacked earthworms, and whether his plants would grow more leaves if he added some.</atomic>
<atomic>Nick added earthworms to the soil in five of his ten pots. After two months of growth, he counted the number of leaves on all ten plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that, on average, the plants with earthworms had 64 leaves, while the plants without earthworms had 51 leaves.</atomic>
<atomic>Nick shared the results of his experiment with his neighbors.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Manny grows tomato plants in his garden. Recently, deer have come into his garden to eat his tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He read that deer do not like garlic and wondered if he could use garlic to stop deer from eating his tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that spraying his tomato plants with garlic water would stop the deer from eating them.</atomic>
<atomic>Manny sprayed half of his tomato plants with garlic water and left the other half unsprayed. He recorded which plants the deer ate every day for two weeks.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the deer avoided the tomato plants sprayed with garlic water but continued to eat the unsprayed plants.</atomic>
<atomic>Manny concluded that garlic water can be used to repel deer from tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his findings with his gardening club.</atomic>

<atomic>She wondered if she could water her petunia plants with gray water.</atomic>
<atomic>Because gray water can contain grease and chemicals, she predicted that plants watered with tap water would have healthier leaves than those watered with gray water.</atomic>

<atomic>When she compared the percentage of dying leaves between the two groups, she found no difference.</atomic>
<atomic>Dana determined that the type of water used did not have a major impact on leaf health.</atomic>
<atomic>So she began watering all of her petunia plants with gray water.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Mia was coaching tennis on a hot summer day. As she hit a ball that had been left on the court, she was surprised to find that it bounced more than the brand new ones she had just opened!</atomic>

<atomic>She thought that it must have something to do with the ball's temperature—the hot asphalt must have warmed it up and made it bouncier than the new ones that had been in an air-conditioned house.</atomic>

<atomic>To test the idea, Mia and her friend gathered nine new tennis balls. They put three in the freezer, left three in the hot sun, and left the remaining three on the kitchen table at room temperature. Thirty minutes later, Mia took all the balls and dropped each one from the top of a 10-foot ladder. Her friend measured how high each one bounced.</atomic>
<atomic>They found that the heated tennis balls bounced the highest, while the frozen ones bounced the lowest.</atomic>
<atomic>They concluded that tennis balls must become bouncier as their temperature rises.</atomic>
<atomic>The next day, Mia shared what she learned with her fellow coaches.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Sophia was getting ready to go for a hike. In order to stay hydrated, she dissolved an electrolyte tablet in a glass of water.</atomic>
<atomic>As she waited for the tablet to fully dissolve, she wondered how she could speed up the reaction rate.</atomic>
<atomic>Sophia predicted that warmer water would cause electrolyte tablets to dissolve more quickly.</atomic>

<atomic>She filled four cups with equal volumes of water. She warmed two of the cups in the microwave and left the other two cups at room temperature. She dropped one tablet into each cup at the same time and used a timer to track how long each tablet took to stop fizzing.</atomic>
<atomic>She averaged the times from each group and noticed that the warmer water almost cut the fizz time in half!</atomic>
<atomic>Sophia concluded that the temperature of the water does affect the reaction rate of electrolyte tablets.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared her results with her hiking group.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Mitch was helping his younger sister use a foam dart launcher that she received for her birthday.</atomic>
<atomic>They wondered what launch angle would cause the foam dart to travel the farthest horizontally.</atomic>

<atomic>They thought that launching with a higher angle to the ground would give the dart more time to travel before hitting the ground and would therefore allow the foam dart to travel farther.</atomic>

<atomic>Mitch and his sister set up an experiment in their backyard. They used a protractor to adjust the launcher to five different angles: 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 75°. They launched three foam darts from each angle and used a measuring tape to determine how far each dart traveled horizontally.</atomic>

<atomic>They then calculated the average for each group and graphed the results. They found that the darts launched at 45° went the farthest, while those launched at 15° and 75° traveled the shortest distance.</atomic>
<atomic>Mitch and his sister shared their results with the friend who had given his sister the launcher.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Linda keeps a vegetable garden in her yard. She likes to germinate her seeds inside before transferring them outside to her garden, but she read that seeds exposed to light germinate more quickly.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered what kind of light would be the best to expose her seeds to indoors for the quickest germination.</atomic>
<atomic>Linda predicted that since red light promotes plant growth, it would also promote seed germination.</atomic>

<atomic>She planted her seeds in three grow beds inside: one lit with a green light, one with a blue light, and one with a red light. She counted how many seeds in each bed germinated after one week.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the bed lit with blue light had the most germinated seeds.</atomic>
<atomic>Linda then predicted that since seeds are not mature plants, they require a different kind of light to germinate.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>As Aaron opened a can of soda, he remembered hearing that soft drinks are fizzy because there is carbon dioxide dissolved in them.</atomic>
<atomic>He knew that sugar and salt dissolve better in hot liquids, so he reasoned that hot soft drinks can dissolve more carbon dioxide and will therefore be fizzier.</atomic>

<atomic>So Aaron got nine identical cans of soda. After opening them, he left three in the refrigerator, three on the kitchen counter, and three outside in the hot sun. Five hours later, he took a sip from each can.</atomic>
<atomic>To his surprise, the cold sodas were the fizziest, while the hot ones had gone flat!</atomic>
<atomic>Based on his experiment, Aaron determined that cold soft drinks are fizzier than hot soft drinks.</atomic>
<atomic>He reasoned that gases, like carbon dioxide, must dissolve differently than solids, like salt and sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>At a cookout the next day, Aaron told his friends to keep their sodas in the shade to help the sodas stay fizzy.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Abby watched her sister change a tire. One bolt seemed stuck, so she took a hollow pipe and put it over the wrench's handle to make it longer.</atomic>
<atomic>Abby wondered why this helped her sister remove the bolts.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that the longer handle allows a person to use less force to turn the wrench.</atomic>

<atomic>To test her idea, Abby and her sister drilled nine small bolts into a wooden board. Abby then attached a spring scale to a normal wrench. As she pulled the spring scale at a right angle to turn the wrench, she measured the force it took to remove a bolt. She repeated this with two more bolts and averaged the three measurements. Then she put a short pipe over the handle and removed the next three bolts. Finally, she put a long pipe over the handle and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>When she compared the three averages, she found that the longest handle took the least force to remove the bolts, while the unmodified wrench took the most.</atomic>
<atomic>Abby concluded that the longer a wrench's handle is, the less force it takes to turn it.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>One summer day, Christy was outside helping her dad spray paint some handles for their kitchen cabinets. When they finished, her dad asked her to take the spray paint inside, because leaving it in the hot sun could cause the canisters to explode. He explained that raising a gas's temperature also raises its pressure. Christy wondered how she could test this relationship.</atomic>
<atomic>Not wanting to cause any explosions, she decided to test it with her dad's car tires.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that the tire pressure would increase after he drove, since the tires would warm up on the road.</atomic>
<atomic>She measured the pressure of each tire on her dad's car before he drove it to work. When he came home, she measured the pressure again.</atomic>
<atomic>She was excited to see that each tire's pressure had increased!</atomic>
<atomic>She concluded that she was correct in predicting that driving raises the pressure in car tires.</atomic>

imageLabel.text: collecting water from one of Plainview's lakes

text.text: <atomic>The members of the Plainview Environmental Club read an article about the acidity of water in lakes and streams.</atomic>
<atomic>The authors of the article found that streams are often less acidic than lakes.</atomic>
<atomic>Plainview County had several streams and lakes, and the club members were curious if the acidity of their streams differed from the acidity of their lakes.</atomic>
<atomic>So, the members measured the acidity of water samples collected from all the streams and lakes in the county.</atomic>
<atomic>The members then made a graph to compare the acidity of the lakes to that of the streams, and they found that the streams were less acidic on average.</atomic>
<atomic>The members published a description of their study and the graph in the county bulletin.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided they would repeat the measurements every year to see if water acidity changed over time.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Clara was playing an apple bobbing game at a party.</atomic>
<atomic>During the game, she began to wonder if a fruit's size is related to whether it floats or sinks.</atomic>
<atomic>She speculated that smaller fruits would float but larger fruits would sink.</atomic>
<atomic>So, Clara gathered five limes, five mangoes, and five pumpkins, placed the fruits in the large tub of water, and recorded whether they floated or sank after five minutes.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the mangoes sank, while the limes and pumpkins floated.</atomic>
<atomic>Since both the smallest and the largest fruits floated, she deduced that size alone does not determine if fruit floats.</atomic>
<atomic>But, since the pumpkins weighed more than the mangoes, Clara also didn't think that heavier fruits would always sink.</atomic>
<atomic>Clara told her friend about her observations.</atomic>
<atomic>Her friend suggested that density might determine if fruits floated, so more dense fruits would sink, and less dense fruits would float.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Brenda bakes bread for a bakery. She stores her bread in clear bins in the back of the bakery, but she sometimes finds mold growing on the bread.</atomic>
<atomic>She wanted to know if exposure to light affects mold growth.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that less mold would grow on her bread if she stored it in dark bins.</atomic>
<atomic>For two weeks, Brenda stored half of her bread in dark bins and the other half in clear bins.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the same amount of mold grew on bread in both types of bins. She also noticed that bread in bins stored closer to the oven had the most mold.</atomic>
<atomic>Based on her experiment, Brenda determined that light did not have a major effect on the total amount of mold that grew on her bread.</atomic>
<atomic>She thought that temperature might affect mold growth and that less mold would grow on bread stored in cold conditions.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Lester took his motorized toy boat to the park with his cousin.</atomic>
<atomic>The boat zipped across the pond, and Lester wondered if adding mass to the boat would affect its speed.</atomic>
<atomic>He didn't think so, since the motor should keep propelling it at the same rate.</atomic>

<atomic>Lester decided to time the boat as it traveled from one side of the pond to the other. He then taped a pebble to the boat and timed it again. Finally, he added a second pebble and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>Lester noticed that as he added mass, the trips took longer. The empty boat took the least time to cross the pond, and the boat with two pebbles took the longest.</atomic>
<atomic>Lester concluded that adding mass does slow down the boat.</atomic>
<atomic>He changed his prediction: The motor must provide a set amount of force, so it can't maintain the same speed as more mass is added.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his results with his aunt and confirmed that the boat's motor exerts a consistent force, so increasing the boat's mass reduces its acceleration.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Mark grows orchids in his home.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the color of light the orchids received could impact how well they grew.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that since the orchids' leaves are green, green light would make them grow the tallest.</atomic>

<atomic>Mark planted three orchids in the same conditions. Once they sprouted, he placed each orchid in a separate dark room and provided each with eight hours of red, green, or blue light. He then measured the growth of each orchid over time.</atomic>
<atomic>He discovered that the orchid with red light grew to 24 inches, the orchid with blue light grew to 20 inches, and the orchid with green light grew to 18 inches.</atomic>
<atomic>Based on his findings, Mark determined that green light did not produce the tallest growth.</atomic>

<atomic>After conducting more research, he predicted that green light made the orchid grow the least because the orchid's green leaves reflect the green light instead of absorbing it for energy.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Barry learned in science class that oil and water do not mix together. His teacher proved this by adding both substances to a container and shaking it. Barry noticed that the oil floated to the top of the container after it had sat untouched for a while.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered, "Could a thick enough oil layer prevent the water from evaporating?"</atomic>
<atomic>He guessed that the thicker the oil layer was, the less water would evaporate because the oil would act as a barrier and stop water molecules from escaping into the air.</atomic>

<atomic>Barry set up nine identical cups and filled each one with an equal amount of water. In the first three cups, he added a thin layer of vegetable oil, just enough to cover the surface. In the next three cups, he added a thicker layer of oil. He did not add any oil to the remaining cups. He left them all on the counter for three days. Then Barry measured the water level in each cup and calculated the average for each group.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the water level was the lowest in the cup with no oil and the highest in the cup with a thick layer of oil.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that a thicker layer of oil does indeed reduce water evaporation more effectively than a thin layer.</atomic>

<atomic>Barry set up nine identical cups and filled each one with an equal amount of water. In the first three cups, he added a thin layer of vegetable oil, just enough to cover the surface. In the next three cups, he added a thicker layer of oil. He did not add any oil to the remaining cups. He left them all on the counter for three days. Then Barry measured the water level in each cup and calculated the average for each group.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the water level was the lowest in the cup with no oil and the highest in the cup with a thick layer of oil.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that a thicker layer of oil does indeed reduce water evaporation more effectively than a thin layer.</atomic>

For one group, he added three earthworms to the soil in each pot. He did not add any earthworms to pots in the other group.
Two months later, Vince counted the number of leaves on each of the ten plants. He compared the number of leaves on the plants in each group.

elements.text: Bonnie had four air plants on her desk that were not growing. She suspected that they needed more water. Bonnie's sister recommended soaking the air plants in a bowl of water once a week. Bonnie's coworker recommended spraying the air plants with a mist of water every day.

Bonnie decided to test both ideas. First, she measured the initial weight of all four air plants. Then, for the next two months, she sprayed two of the plants with a mist of water each day. She watered the two remaining plants by soaking them in water once a week. Finally, Bonnie measured the weight of the plants again and calculated the change in weight for each plant.

mainText.text: Sue built an electric circuit: she used wires to connect a battery to a light bulb, the light bulb to a small piece of copper, and the copper back to the battery. When the circuit was complete, the light turned on. Sue observed the brightness of the light for five seconds. She then replaced the copper with a piece of iron of equal size and noted whether the light became brighter or dimmer. Sue built three more of the same type of circuit. She repeated the tests with each circuit. Sue recorded whether the circuits produced brighter light when the circuit included copper or when the circuit included iron.

contents.text: Identify the question that Sue's experiment can best answer.

choices.text: Do circuits that include iron produce dimmer light than circuits that include copper?
Can light bulbs stay lit longer when circuits include copper or when circuits include iron?

mainText.text: Logan made six batches of muffins over the course of one day. He used whole wheat flour in three of the batches and white flour in the other three batches. He divided the batter into muffin tins, using two ounces of batter per muffin. He baked the muffins in a 350°F oven for 20 minutes. He compared the volumes of the muffins made with whole wheat flour to the volumes of the muffins made with white flour.

choices.text: Does the type of flour used in the muffins affect the number of muffins that turn brown after 30 minutes in the oven?
Do muffins made with white flour have larger volumes than muffins made with whole wheat flour?

mainText.text: Reggie used a dropper to put equal-sized drops of pure water, one at a time, onto a penny. The drops stayed together and formed a dome on the penny's surface. Reggie recorded the number of drops he could add before the water spilled over the edge of the penny. Then, he rinsed and dried the penny, and repeated the test using water mixed with hand soap. He repeated these trials on nine additional pennies. Reggie compared the average number of pure water drops to the average number of water drops mixed with hand soap that he could add to a penny before the water spilled over.

imageLabel.text: a dome of water on the surface of a penny

contents.text: Identify the question that Reggie's experiment can best answer.

choices.text: Can pennies hold more drops of water mixed with dish soap or water mixed with hand soap?
Can pennies hold more drops of pure water or water mixed with hand soap?

lessons.name: Understand an experimental protocol about plant growth

pieces.text: The instructions for how to carry out a science experiment can be found in an

. An experimental protocol often includes the list of materials you need for the experiment. The protocol also includes the procedure, which is a list of steps for carrying out the experiment. Some experimental protocols include data tables for recording the results of the experiment.

header.text: The experimental protocol below is for an experiment investigating tomato plant growth. Read through the experimental protocol, then answer the question below.

elements.text: Pour the soil into the large plastic container and add water until the soil is moist.
Fill the pots with the moistened soil. Label each pot with a number from 1 through 10.
Plant one tomato plant in each pot.
In pots 6 through 10, add two earthworms just beneath the soil surface.
Place all of the pots next to each other in a warm, sunny area.
Once a day, give each plant four ounces of water.
After three months, count the number of tomatoes on each plant.
Record your results in the following tables.

content.text: Plants grown in soil without earthworms
Plants grown in soil with earthworms

. An experimental protocol often includes the list of materials you need for the experiment. The protocol also includes the procedure, which is a list of steps for carrying out the experiment. Some experimental protocols include data tables for recording the results of the experiment.
The experimental protocol below is for an experiment about evaporation. This experiment looks at

, or the amount of salt dissolved in water. The experiment investigates how salinity affects evaporation. The experiment tests tap water, which contains very little salt, and water mixed with different amounts of table salt.

The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will remain after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

contents.text: In this experiment, the independent variable is the amount of time each beaker is under a heat lamp. The amount of time spent under a heat lamp may affect the rate of evaporation, or how quickly the water evaporates.
The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will be remaining after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

header.text: So, the experiment can answer this question:

content.text: Does the amount of time under a heat lamp affect the rate of evaporation?

header.text: The experiment cannot answer these questions:

content.text: Does the salinity of water affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, all the beakers are filled with tap water. So, this experiment does not test the effect of salinity.

content.text: Does the amount of time under a heat lamp affect the water temperature?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, beakers are heated by heat lamps for different amounts of time. However, data on water temperature are not collected or recorded. So, this experiment does not test the effect of time under a heat lamp on water temperature.

contents.text: In this experiment, the independent variable is the salinity of the water. The salinity of the water may affect the rate of evaporation, or how quickly the water evaporates.
The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will remain after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

header.text: So, the experiment can answer this question:

content.text: Does the salinity of the water affect the rate of evaporation?

header.text: The experiment cannot answer these questions:

content.text: Does the temperature of the water affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, the temperature of the water in each beaker is the same. So, this experiment does not test the effect of temperature.

content.text: Does the size of the beaker affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, the beakers are identical, or the same. So, this experiment does not test the effect of using beakers of different sizes.
